standard.title: Discuss and reflect with peers
standard.description: use non-verbal, spoken and written exchanges to discuss, plan and reflect on activities, events and experiences with peers
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can engage in modelled non-verbal, spoken and written exchanges to organise activities in familiar contexts (AC9LS8EC03). They have not yet discussed, planned and reflected on activities and experiences in ways that require extended planning, negotiation and post-activity reflection in the target language.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use non-verbal, spoken and written exchanges in the target language to discuss, plan and reflect on activities, events and experiences with peers — including managing multi-stage processes and negotiating outcomes.

nodes.label: Planning and negotiating collaboratively
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use the target language to plan and negotiate with peers through a multi-stage process — assigning roles, making decisions and managing adjustments.
nodes.minimum_width: Participate in a collaborative planning task in the target language that involves at least two stages (e.g. proposal, decision, assignment of roles).
nodes.typical_width: Plan, negotiate and execute a collaborative project or event using spoken, written and digital exchanges in the target language; manage disagreements and adjustments through negotiation; use appropriate language for proposing, agreeing, disagreeing and revising.
wider: Plan and execute a real or simulated event (e.g. a class celebration, a fundraiser, a trip) using the target language as the primary medium throughout — from planning to evaluation
Compare how negotiation and planning language conventions differ in formal and informal contexts in the target language

response_modes.reason: Multi-stage collaborative planning integrates discussion strategies (EC02), functional classroom language (EC02 Y7-8) and transactional exchange skills (EC03 Y7-8) into a sustained, purposeful communicative task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine planning contexts, not simulated planning with predetermined outcomes.

success_criteria: Participates in at least two planning stages of a collaborative task using target language for proposal, negotiation or decision
Manages at least one adjustment or disagreement during the task using target language rather than reverting to English

nodes.label: Non-verbal communication and meaning-making
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and use non-verbal communication strategies in the target language context and reflect on their role in meaning-making across cultural contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two non-verbal strategies used in an observed or participated-in target language interaction and reflect on their contribution to meaning.
nodes.typical_width: Participate in exchanges that require coordinating non-verbal, spoken and written elements; reflect on how non-verbal conventions differ across cultural contexts; identify where non-verbal communication can clarify or obscure meaning across cultural boundaries.
wider: Participate in a charades or mime scenario in the target language and reflect explicitly on what non-verbal communication conveys vs what requires language
Research non-verbal communication conventions in the target language community and compare with Australian English conventions — present findings to peers

response_modes.reason: Non-verbal convention awareness requires exposure across varied interaction contexts. Single examples do not generalise — students need to encounter how gesture, posture, silence and proxemics operate differently across social contexts in the target language community.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Non-verbal communication is the concrete, embodied dimension of intercultural understanding. At Y9-10, explicit reflection on non-verbal conventions deepens the cultural dimension of the Languages curriculum in a way that is directly experiential rather than purely analytical.
success_criteria: Can identify at least two non-verbal strategies used in a target language interaction and explain their communicative function
Can identify at least one non-verbal convention that differs between the target language community and Australian English

nodes.label: Reflecting on activities and experiences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can reflect in the target language on completed activities and experiences — identifying what went well, what was challenging and what they would change.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce one reflective exchange (spoken or written) in the target language about a completed activity, identifying at least one strength and one area for improvement.
nodes.typical_width: Reflect on activities, events and experiences using spoken, written or digital exchanges; discuss what was challenging, surprising or significant; connect reflections to personal or cultural learning.
wider: Maintain a reflective journal or digital record in the target language across a unit of work — trace developing language and cultural understanding over time

Reflect on the experience of using the target language in a real or near-real context (e.g. interacting with a speaker, watching authentic media) — identify what was possible and what was beyond current capacity

response_modes.reason: Reflection in a second language requires students to produce extended, self-referential text — a cognitively demanding task. Reflection frames and sentence starters that scaffold the reflective move (first... then... I noticed... I would change...) reduce the cognitive load and allow genuine reflection rather than surface description.

success_criteria: Produces a reflection in the target language that identifies at least one strength and one challenge from a completed activity
Reflection goes beyond description of events — includes at least one evaluative or interpretive statement
